summary: San Marino has no border controls of its own — you must travel through Italy to enter, so Schengen rules decide everything: EU/EEA citizens and Schengen visa-waiver nationals walk straight in, while other travelers need an Italian Schengen visa.

primarySources.name: San Marino Department of Foreign Affairs

AF.notes: San Marino has no border controls of its own. Entry runs through Italy, so an Italian Schengen short-stay visa is required.

AL.notes: Visa-free with a biometric passport under Schengen rules, entering through Italy — 90 days in any 180-day period. ETIAS authorization will be required once mandatory. San Marino itself allows 30 days without a permit of stay; to stay longer, apply to the Gendarmeria's Foreigners Office within those 30 days.

tips.text: You have to travel through Italy to reach San Marino. The UK FCDO says there are no border controls to pass on entry, but your passport must carry a valid entry stamp from a Schengen country.
Days spent in San Marino count against your 90/180-day Schengen allowance in practice, since entry and exit run through Italy without separate controls.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for San Marino?
faq.answer: San Marino issues no visas and runs no border controls. Entry is governed by Schengen rules through Italy. If you can enter Italy, whether visa-free or on a Schengen visa, you can visit San Marino.

faq.question: Does visiting San Marino use up a single-entry Schengen visa?
faq.answer: In practice no. There are no controls on the Italy–San Marino border, so you never formally exit the Schengen Area; travelers on single-entry visas visit without any issue.

faq.question: How long can I stay in San Marino?
faq.answer: For visa-waiver and Schengen-visa travelers, your stay is bounded by your Schengen allowance — 90 days in any 180 — since you come and go through Italy. If you stay in San Marino for more than 30 days, you must go to the Gendarmeria's Foreigners Office (Ufficio Stranieri) within those 30 days and apply for a permit of stay.
